title: {{NAME}} and the Tiniest Teammate in the Tournament
moral: Underestimating someone because of their size is always the mistake of the person who does it.

pages.content:
The Gear-and-Wing Tournament was the only competition in any league that had ever officially permitted non-standard team members, following a series of very long meetings at the Interspecies Football Confederation that {{NAME}} had not attended but had heard about extensively. The result was a mixed-category bracket where humans, robots, and fairies could register on the same team, provided the team kept below a total body-mass limit that everyone agreed was somewhat arbitrary but was nonetheless the rule.

{{NAME}}'s team, the Tangerine Gears, had a problem: their registered robot teammate, a compact midfielder called SWIFT-9, had developed a joint fault the morning of the tournament and was sitting in the repair bay with his left leg off and a rueful expression on his sensor panel. The team was one player short with forty minutes to the opening match.

The fairy appeared at the touchline while {{NAME}} was reviewing the roster with a creased face and a worse feeling in the stomach. She was called Nix, and she was the size of a sparrow, and she said, very directly: 'I play midfield. I am available. And I am considerably faster than your robot.' She did not say this with arrogance. She said it with the calm precision of someone reporting a measurement they have taken carefully. SWIFT-9, from the repair bay, said via comms: 'She is statistically correct. I checked her previous recorded pace when she entered the facility.' Everyone looked at SWIFT-9. He rotated his remaining leg slightly. 'Data is data,' he added.

pages.content:
The opposing team in the first match, the Iron Comet, were not rude about Nix. They were worse than rude: they were amused.

Their captain, a broad-shouldered robot called CRUX-7, surveyed the Tangerine Gears' lineup at the pre-match handshake and his gaze passed over Nix, who was standing on {{NAME}}'s shoulder for the occasion, as though she were a decorative pin. 'Interesting choice,' he said, in the voice of someone who has already decided what they think. Nix met his sensor-eyes with complete composure. 'You should worry less about our choices and more about your left-flank gap,' she said pleasantly. CRUX-7's sensor panel flickered. He had not expected a reply.

{{NAME}} leaned down to Nix during the team huddle, voice low. 'Are you sure about this? It's a big pitch.' Nix looked up with an expression so steady and certain it made {{NAME}} feel immediately that the question had been the wrong question. 'The pitch is the same size for everyone,' she said. 'The difference is how you use it.' She was approximately one-quarter the size of the ball. {{NAME}} made a note to stop underestimating people before being explicitly corrected and just never do it in the first place.

pages.content:
Nix was electric.

Not metaphorically: her wings created a faint static charge when she accelerated to full speed, and the first time she intercepted an Iron Comet pass the opposing winger genuinely startled backwards as though he'd touched a live wire. She was in three places in sequence so quickly that it temporarily looked like three Nixes, and CRUX-7's tactical sensors spent the first fifteen minutes trying to find a category for her and settling unhappily on 'anomaly.'

She couldn't shoot at goal herself: at four inches tall, kicking a full-size ball required a running jump and produced a tap rather than a strike. She knew this with absolute self-awareness and never attempted it. Instead she was pure creation: setting up angles, drawing defenders, delivering passes with a precision that came from being able to see the entire pitch from three feet in the air. Every ball she gave {{NAME}} arrived at exactly the right weight, moving in exactly the right direction, like a gift that had already thought about what you needed.

{{NAME}} scored twice in the first half, both from Nix assists. CRUX-7 called three tactical timeouts. The Iron Comet changed formation twice. Nix responded to each change in roughly twelve seconds. The Tangerine Gears led two-nil at half time and the fairy-section of the crowd, who had been a small and polite group at the start of the match, had considerably expanded.

pages.content:
The tournament final, played three hours later after the Tangerine Gears had won two more matches in the bracket, came down to the last minute of extra time at one-all.

SWIFT-9's leg had been repaired by an enthusiastic mechanic in the repair bay and he'd been cleared to come on as a substitute in the second half of the final, moving with his characteristic economical precision, occupying space tactically rather than covering it physically. He and Nix were an unexpected combination: the robot thinking seven moves ahead in logical sequences, the fairy reading the emotional rhythm of the match, the two of them complementing each other in ways that neither could have managed alone.

With thirty seconds left, Nix went down. Not injured: exhausted. She had flown the equivalent of six kilometres in three hours and her wings were moving at a fraction of their usual speed. She landed on the pitch and stood, small and absolutely determined, her glow dimmed but present.

The ball fell to {{NAME}} at midfield. One defender between goal and everything else. SWIFT-9 calling the angle from the right. Nix, from the ground, pointing with one small hand toward a gap that opened and would close in two seconds. {{NAME}} threaded it through: not a power shot, a precise one, placed where SWIFT-9's calculation and Nix's instinct had agreed it should go. It arrived at the goal corner like something that had always known its destination. Final whistle.

pages.content:
The medal ceremony required a creative solution for Nix's medal, which was produced by the tournament jeweller in under fifteen minutes and was the exact right size, made of copper and fairy-fire, and hung on a chain of spun silk no thicker than a breath. SWIFT-9 accepted his medal with both hands and turned it over three times in his precise fingers, examining it with the attention of someone who was storing it as a particularly significant data point.

CRUX-7 found {{NAME}} and Nix in the post-match gathering and extended his hand with the specific posture of a robot whose sensor-panel was running something in the vicinity of respect. 'She was not an anomaly,' he said. 'She was a strategy.' Nix accepted this with a small nod. 'I know,' she said. 'I always was.'

{{NAME}} sat on the changing-room bench later with the gold medal in both hands and Nix asleep across one knee, her wings folded and her glow a soft, steady ember. SWIFT-9 sat on the adjacent bench, charging, his sensor panel running its quiet maintenance cycle.

Three of you, {{NAME}} thought. All different. All necessary. All excellent.

The stadium lights dimmed outside and the night came in gently. Sleep now, teammate. Close your eyes and let the medal be heavy and good in your hands. And in the morning, SWIFT-9 will have calculated six new set pieces, and Nix will have thoughts about all of them.
